title: Group Moving Discounts: How Two Neighbors Moving out of the Same Condo Complex Can Save Big with Active Movers
excerpt: When two units in the same compound move the same week, one truck and one elevator slot often costs less than two separate bookings—here’s how to split the quote fairly.
content:
Group moving discounts: neighbors leaving the same compound

If you and a neighbor in the same condo or housing association are both moving out during the same week, you are paying twice for things that only need to happen once: truck mobilization from our yard, security registration at the gate, and—most importantly—the freight elevator block your building management allows. Active Movers can structure a sequential same-day move or a shared truck route so both households save on mobilization while keeping separate inventories and insurance.

This works often in Ayat, Friendship City–style compounds, and dense Bole blocks where management prefers one vendor and one elevator booking instead of two panicked end-of-month trucks.

Economics of a shared move

Mobilization is the fixed cost of getting the right truck and crew to your gate. When two similar-sized units move back-to-back, the second load typically costs less than a fresh dispatch because the crew is already on site, blankets are staged, and the truck is warm. Savings vary by volume, but neighbors often share 2,000–6,000 ETB of mobilization and management fees compared with two unrelated bookings—always confirmed on a written quote, not a verbal guess.

  • One mobilization fee — one truck serves two units (sequential loads) or one long slot with two stops.
  • One elevator window — back-to-back freight hours negotiated with management (critical in high-rise blocks).
  • Bulk packing materials — shared box bundles for both units when both choose packing service.
  • Single gate process — one security list, one compound fee where applicable.
  • Second-unit discount — crew already on site; no second trip from depot.

Coordination requirements

Both households need a combined walkthrough or video survey so truck size and hours reflect both inventories. We stagger loading—Unit A out first, then Unit B—or color-code cartons (BLUE vs GREEN) so nothing crosses at the elevator. Payment can stay on two contracts with a shared mobilization line item, or one master invoice with a documented split.

When sharing a truck works

Best fit: similar volume (two studios, two two-bedroom condos), moves on the same day or consecutive slots, and destinations along the same corridor (e.g. Ayat to Bole, not Ayat to Sululta opposite directions). Poor fit: one villa and one studio—the truck size is driven by the larger job, and the smaller home may still need its own trip. In that case ask for a group admin discount on permits and scheduling instead of forcing one overloaded truck.

Neighbor agreement in writing

Agree before moving day: split formula (50/50 mobilization vs proportional by volume), who pays if the elevator runs long because of one household’s delay, and that each move keeps its own declared value for insurance. Active Movers can attach a short split annex to both quotes.

Compound politics

Tell management and security you are using one company for two units—they often appreciate fewer truck days. Give iddir or neighbors a courteous heads-up if the truck will occupy the gate longer than a single move; one notice beats two separate peak-week surprises.

Conclusion

Two neighbors in the same compound can save real money by coordinating one professional operation instead of duplicate trucks and elevator fights—especially before end-of-month rush. Plan together, get one combined survey, and split the savings transparently.
